newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: UAE names new government but no major policy change.
newsitem.headline: UAE names new government but no major policy change.

text.p: United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan on Tuesday named a new oil minister in the country's first cabinet reshuffle in six years.
The official news agency WAM said he appointed Obaid bin Saif al-Nasseri, a member of a prominent Abu Dhabi family born in 1952, to head the petroleum and mineral resources ministry.

Nasseri, who has held a number of senior posts in the financial sector including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and the National Bank of Abu Dhabi replaced Rakad bin Salem bin Rakad, who had been acting oil minister since June 1995. Rakad kept his job as public works and housing minister.

The position of oil minister is not crucial in the UAE, where oil policy is determined by the Higher Petroleum Council chaired by Sheikh Khalifa bin Zaid al-Nahayan, crown prince of Abu Dhabi and heir apparent to Sheikh Zaid.
A government official said: "There is no change in policy. It was a re-structuring operation."
There were eight new faces in the cabinet.
Sheikh Zaid appointed a new minister of economy and commerce -- Sheikh Fahem bin Sultan al-Qassimi, former secretary-general of the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council.
Other key ministers in the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Maktoum bin Rashid al-Maktoum -- defence, foreign affairs and finance -- were reappointed.
Sheikh Zaid, who is in his late 70s, named one of his sons, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zaid al-Nahayan, 24, as minister of information and culture.

Since 1990, several ministers had been changed but this was the first major reshuffle of the cabinet in the oil-rich Gulf Arab state, a member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
The UAE has an OPEC quota of 2.161 million barrels per day.

"There were no big surprises as he retained the key ministers, signalling a continuation of policy," said one political source. "It was a long-awaited reshuffle to fill the portfolios that were vacated over the past years."

The UAE, a federation of seven emirates, was formed in 1971 when Britain unilaterally withdrew its military protection from the impoverished Trucial States -- Abu Dhabi, Ajman, Dubai, Fujairah, Ras al-Khaimah, Sharjah and Umm al-Quwain -- which had subsisted on fishing, pearl diving and trade.
Sheikh Zaid has been president since the country was formed.
The UAE is now one of the world's wealthiest countries with oil revenue of $9 billion a year and sufficient crude in the ground to last a century.

The highest federal authority in the UAE, where there are no political parties, is the Supreme Council composed of the rulers of the seven emirates. The Federal National Council, appointed by the rulers, has a consultative role.
